=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-2 Trade Secret Assertion.docx ===
BEFORE THE GEORGIA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION

Georgia Power Company
Docket No. 56002
Georgia Power Company’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Georgia Power’s Company’s Application for the Certification, Decertification, and Amended Demand-Side Management Plan
STF-PIA Data Request Set No. 22 

BASIS FOR THE ASSERTION THAT THE 
INFORMATION SUBMITTED IS A TRADE SECRET


	As part of Georgia Power Company’s Georgia Power Company’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Georgia Power’s Company’s Application for the Certification, Decertification, and Amended Demand-Side Management Plan filed in Docket No. 56002 (“Georgia Power Company’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Georgia Power’s Company’s Application for the Certification, Decertification, and Amended Demand-Side Management Plan”), Georgia Power Company (“Georgia Power” or the “Company”) submits to the Georgia Public Service Commission its response to STF-PIA-22-2 (“Response”). In the Response, the Company has provided specific wildfire risk and operational response information (the “Information”). All such information constitutes trade secret information of the Southern Company, Georgia Power, and its affiliates and is therefore protected from public disclosure under Commission Rule 515-3-1-.11.

	The Information derives economic value from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use. Specifically, the Information contains detailed wildfire risk assessment results and the operational thresholds, alert levels, and response protocols the Company uses to identify and respond to elevated fire conditions, including the criteria under which facilities may be de-energized. Public disclosure of this Information would allow third parties to identify the specific conditions and locations in which the Company’s facilities are most vulnerable and would compromise the security of critical electric infrastructure and the safety of the public. The Information further reflects substantial investment by Southern Company and Georgia Power in developing these assessments, tools, and protocols, and its disclosure would allow others to obtain that value without comparable investment, putting Georgia Power at a competitive and economic disadvantage. Competitors are not required to disclose similar information and to require Georgia Power to do so would put it at an economic disadvantage.

	The Information is subject to substantial procedures to maintain its secrecy. Only select Georgia Power and Southern Company Services personnel are granted access to the Information. Those personnel receive access only on a “need to know” basis. Parties outside the Company who have been granted access to the Information, if any, have been required to sign confidentiality agreements with respect to the Information.

=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-6.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-6

Question: 

Does the Company currently utilize any advanced technologies (e.g. automated fault detection devices or programs) for reducing the likelihood of wildfire ignition from transmission and distribution facilities? Are there plans to add these technologies?

Response:

The Company utilizes automated fault detection and fault clearing technologies on its transmission and distribution facilities. Additionally, the Company's fault location, isolation, and service restoration schemes (i.e., self-healing networks) segment an outage and re-route and restore service in less than a minute in cases where these schemes are used. For certain transmission and distribution devices equipped with supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) capabilities, the Company has the ability to disable automatic reclosing when it deems appropriate based on fire conditions. While these technologies are deployed primarily for reliability purposes given the more pertinent threat, the secondary benefit of reducing wildfire ignition opportunities remains.

=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-11.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-11

Question: 

How does the Company recover a personal injury or property damage caused by wildfire? Please explain the insurance plans, if any, and explain how it best works for the ratepayers.

Response:

Georgia Power is self-insured for third-party bodily injury and property damage claims and maintains excess liability insurance as part of Southern Company’s liability insurance program. The liability insurance includes coverage for third-party bodily injury and property damage liability claims due to wildfire. In addition, Georgia Power maintains property insurance coverage, which insures damage to our generation and substation assets if caused by wildfire. The Company is self-insured for transmission and distribution lines and poles as is usual and customary in this industry.  Georgia Power’s insurance arrangement helps ensure that affected parties can recover for relevant wildfire related losses, while protecting ratepayers from major rate increases due to wildfire damages.

=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-9 PUBLIC DISCLOSURE.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-9

Question: 

Please provide data on past wildfire events which triggered action by the Company, if any, from January 2022 to the present date.
Date of event
Facility and equipment damaged
Length of event
Location / area / counties
Customers affected
Original cause (weather, human, utility, vegetation in ROW, vegetation out of ROW, vehicle, etc.)
Company response
Event response cost
Post event assessment

Response:

The Company does not track wildfire as a distinct cause classification within its outage management records. As a result, a comprehensive listing of wildfire events for the period from January 2022 to the present is not readily available. However, the Company has identified the following wildfire event and provides the information below as a representative example of how it evaluates and responds to wildfire conditions that may affect Company facilities.


Date of event - 04/21/26 – 04/26/26.
Facility and equipment damaged – no Company equipment was damaged.
Length of event – The length of the event was about 5 days for the Company.
Location / area / counties – 2 simultaneous wildfires: Clinch/ Echols County & Brantley County.
Customers affected – The Company had no customers affected.
Original cause (weather, human, utility, vegetation in ROW, vegetation out of ROW, vehicle, etc.) The Pineland Road Fire and the Highway 82 Brantley Fire occurred outside the Company's service territory and had no impact on Company facilities. The Company is not the investigating authority for these events and defers to the appropriate state agency with respect to cause determinations.
Company response –The Company supported fire response efforts by coordinating resources from multiple organizations to conduct aerial and ground-based monitoring activities. As a precautionary measure, the Company de-energized certain 230 kV facilities; however, no customer load was impacted. Company personnel also harrowed and improved rights-of-way near transmission facilities to reduce available fuel and help limit fire spread. In addition, the Company evaluated other nearby assets, performed system studies, and developed contingency plans to de-energize additional facilities if conditions were warranted. Following confirmation that the fire no longer posed a threat to Company facilities and completion of comprehensive inspections, the affected facilities were re-energized. No damage to Company assets occurred.
Event response cost - REDACTED 
The team worked across generation, transmission, and corporate support to assess its response to this event. Through this process, the team identified the importance of continuing to improve coordination amongst local and state teams in communicating on fire response. Resources worked well once communication was coordinated. The Company also identified response engagement, including better awareness of the varying levels of fire response amongst team members as an area of emphasis. Importantly, understanding local government and charitable resources available to aid in responding to customers or individuals impacted by fire in the local communities is another area of emphasis. The Company continues to ensure emphasis on quality control of the Company’s right of way or other high-risk habitats for fire.

Response:


Wildfires are addressed within the Company’s existing operating, emergency, and storm response processes rather than through a separate wildfire response organization. Elevated fire conditions increase situational awareness and can prompt operational adjustments, as described in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-22-4(g).

The Company currently has 150 weather stations deployed across the system and continues to evaluate locations where additional units may add value. These units provide ground level weather data for the Company’s predictive tools, namely the Storm Prediction, Estimated Restoration Times and Reporting (“SPEAR”) tool to forecast a 5-day wildfire projection. Additionally, the Company’s in-house meteorologist supports real-time monitoring of weather and fire conditions. These tools are further described in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-22-4(g).

The Company’s vegetation management contractors perform the work plans and inspections described in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-22-4(d). The Company does not maintain vegetation management contractors dedicated to wildfire response.

During an active fire, the Company coordinates with state and local agencies, as further described in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-22-4(b). === DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-2.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-2

Question: 

How does the Company currently determine whether wildfires are identified as an ‘extreme weather risk’ in its service territory?

Response:
The Company produces a five-day forecast of wildfire conditions over its service territory and maintains a corresponding Wildfire Operational Alert matrix to guide operational response in areas forecast to observe conditions favorable for wildfire ignition and spread. The forecast is evaluated using the Company's Fire Potential Index (FPI), which assigns one of five fire potential levels based on forecast conditions. The resulting fire potential level is used in conjunction with the Wildfire Operational Alert matrix to determine the appropriate level of preparedness and response.
 Please see STF-PIA-22-2 Attachment for the matrix.

The Wildfire Operational Alert matrix provides a structured framework for evaluating identified wildfire risks and determining the appropriate level of operational response across the service territory. The FPI assesses fire risk over the next five days and provides a consistent basis for escalating preparedness and response activities as conditions warrant.

The FPI is calibrated using established thresholds in weather conditions and fire science, together with historical environment data in the vicinity of large fires that have occurred in the Southeast. By incorporating these factors, the FPI is designed to reflect conditions and wildfire characteristics relevant to the company's geographic region and operating environment. The index consists of five distinct levels representing increasing degrees of fire potential. Each level is associated with a corresponding set of actions and response measures, allowing the company to adjust its posture as fire conditions change.

Together, the Wildfire Operational Alert matrix and FPI provide a coordinated approach for identifying, evaluating, and responding to wildfire risk. The five FPI levels and the corresponding actions associated with each level are outlined in the attached matrix.





=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-1.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-1

Question: 

How does the Company continue to ‘evaluate opportunities to mitigate identified extreme weather risk’ as stated in the 2022 IRP DR response to STF-PIA-3-24?

Response:

As stated in the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-24, the Company continues to evaluate opportunities to mitigate identified extreme weather risk on an ongoing basis. Extreme weather risk is evaluated within the Company’s established design, asset management, vegetation management, resiliency, and operational programs rather than through a separate, standalone program.
 
Through these processes, the Company considers operational experience from weather events on the system and developments across the industry, including through participation in industry organizations. The Company applies that experience through its design standards, which meet or exceed the National Electrical Safety Code, and uses weather and system data to identify risks and prioritize investments. The Company also participates in industry organizations, including the Southeastern Electric Exchange, the Edison Electric Institute, and the Association of Edison Illuminating Companies.
 
Where a specific risk is identified, the Company evaluates and, where appropriate, implements targeted mitigation. Examples include generation and critical substation winterization, elevation of substation control houses, transmission and substation design criteria that account for extreme wind and ice loading, burn guards, distribution storm hardening, and vegetation management. Wildfire risk is evaluated within this same framework and is further described in the Company’s responses to STF-PIA-22-2, STF-PIA-22-3, and STF-PIA-22-4.




=== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-PIA-22 PD/STF-PIA-22-10.docx ===
STF-PIA-22-10

Question: 

Does the company have any public awareness programs regarding wildfire- related risks? How does the Company engage with other Community based organizations? Please explain if any.

Response:

Yes. The Company’s Right-of-Way Services team periodically offers controlled burn education in conjunction with the Georgia Forestry Commission and the Georgia Forestry Association.
 
The Company’s engagement with outside organizations on wildfire-related topics is conducted primarily through those organizations. In addition, the Company’s Land Management organization is conducting a wildfire recap session with the Georgia Forestry Commission concerning the 2026 South Georgia wildfires.
